standard_text: Identify the unit rate or constant of proportionality in tables, graphs, equations, and verbal descriptions of proportional relationships.

progression.narrative: This standard asks students to pull one number, the unit rate or constant of proportionality k, out of tables, graphs, equations, and verbal descriptions of proportional relationships. The on-grade work moves from deciding whether a relationship is proportional at all, to recognizing k when the pair (1, r) is handed over, to computing k as y divided by x, including the cases where k or the quantities are fractions. Students who stall here are usually missing arithmetic from well below grade seven, most often the meaning of division as equal sharing and the fact that a fraction is itself a division. Intervention should rebuild those foundations first, then the grade six skills of dividing to find a per one amount and dividing with fractions, and only then return to proportional relationships.

steps.rationale: You cannot find a constant of proportionality in a relationship that does not have one. Telling proportional (constant ratio, passes through the origin) from non-proportional (a flat fee, a head start) is the gate every later step depends on.
The gentlest way to name k is when the relationship already shows the pair (1, r): the constant is just r. Recognizing k when it is handed to you comes before computing it.

The core of the standard: when no (1, r) pair is shown, compute the constant as y divided by x from any table row or verbal description — including the common case where the answer is not a whole number.
The spec's 'difficult' band uses fractional quantities (1/2 mile in 7 minutes). Dividing a fraction by a whole number to get a unit rate is a distinct mechanical hurdle that deserves its own step.

The standard names equations and graphs as representations. In y = kx the constant is the coefficient; on a graph it is the y-value at x = 1. Reading k off these two representations is a recognition skill separate from computing it.
The Above-proficiency payoff: once k is in hand, explain what it means in the story and use y = kx to predict a value the table never listed. This is why the constant is worth finding.

skills.name: Divide a total into equal groups

prerequisite_skill.description: Interpret division as sharing a total equally and find the size of one group, facts within 100.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: 12 cookies are shared equally among 3 friends. How many cookies does each friend get?

skills.i_do_script: Division answers the question: if I share this total equally, how big is one group? Watch: 12 cookies shared among 3 friends. I draw 3 circles, one per friend, and deal the cookies out one at a time, around and around, until the 12 are gone. Each circle ends up with 4 cookies, so 12 divided by 3 is 4. The total gets split, the number of groups does the splitting, and the answer is the size of ONE group. That one-group amount is the whole point of dividing.

canonical_error.pattern: Multiplies the two numbers instead of dividing, or answers with the number of groups
canonical_error.example: For '12 cookies shared among 3 friends' the student writes 12 x 3 = 36, or answers 3
canonical_error.why: The student sees two numbers and reaches for the operation that makes a bigger number, or reports the group count instead of the group size. Sharing never makes more cookies; dealing them into circles shows each friend gets fewer than the total.

skills.item_template: A total shared into equal groups (facts within 100, no remainders). Student finds the size of one group. Short numeric response fluency bank.

sample_items.stem: 12 cookies are shared equally among 3 friends. How many cookies does each friend get?
20 stickers are shared equally among 4 kids. How many stickers each?
15 divided by 3
24 crayons are put into 6 equal boxes. How many crayons in each box?
30 divided by 5
16 markers are split equally into 2 cups. How many markers in each cup?
27 divided by 3
40 apples are packed equally into 8 bags. How many apples in each bag?

redirect_script.stop: Did sharing make more cookies or fewer for each person?
redirect_script.prompt: Draw one circle for each friend and deal the total out one at a time until it is gone. Count what lands in ONE circle. That count is the answer, and it has to be smaller than the total.
redirect_script.praise: You dealt the total into equal groups and counted one group, that is exactly what division means.

vocabulary.definition: Split a total into equal groups.
Groups that all hold the same amount.

next_steps.if_fail: Review grade 3 division as equal sharing with counters (deal a total into circles and count one group).

worked_example_script.text: Draw 3 circles labeled friend 1, friend 2, friend 3. Deal 12 counters into them one at a time, around and around.
How many counters ended up in each circle? Did every circle get the same amount?
Each circle holds 4, so 12 divided by 3 is 4. The 12 is the total, the 3 is how many groups, and the 4 is the size of one group.
If a student answers 36 or 3, hand them the counters: deal them out and count one circle. Sharing cannot make more than you started with.
Your turn: deal 20 counters into 4 circles. How many in each?

skills.name: Interpret a fraction as division

prerequisite_skill.description: Understand that the fraction a/b means a divided by b, and use it to share a whole-number amount.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: 3 sandwiches are shared equally by 4 people. How much sandwich does each person get?

skills.i_do_script: A fraction IS a division problem: a/b means a divided by b. Watch: 3 sandwiches shared equally by 4 people. I cut each sandwich into 4 equal pieces, so every sandwich gives each person one piece, one fourth. Three sandwiches give each person three fourths. So 3 divided by 4 equals 3/4, no leftover mystery. The top number is the total being shared and the bottom number is how many ways it is split. This works even when the total is smaller than the number of sharers.

canonical_error.pattern: Flips the division because the divisor is bigger, writing b/a instead of a/b
canonical_error.example: For 3 divided by 4 the student writes 4/3, saying you cannot divide 3 by 4
canonical_error.why: The student believes the bigger number must be divided by the smaller. But sharing 3 sandwiches among 4 people is possible, each person just gets less than one whole. The sandwich picture shows each share is 3/4, not 4/3.

skills.item_template: A whole-number division written as a fraction, or a sharing story with a total smaller than or near the number of sharers. Student writes the fraction or the share. Short response fluency bank.

sample_items.stem: Write 3 divided by 4 as a fraction.
3 sandwiches are shared equally by 4 people. How much does each person get?
Write the fraction 1/2 as a division problem.
Write 5 divided by 8 as a fraction.
2 brownies are shared equally by 5 kids. How much brownie does each kid get?
Write the fraction 7/10 as a division problem.
Write 4 divided by 5 as a fraction.
Write 9 divided by 2 as a mixed number.

redirect_script.stop: Which number is being shared, and how many ways is it split?
redirect_script.prompt: The total being shared goes on top and the number of sharers goes on the bottom. Cut each whole into that many pieces and give one piece from each whole to each person. Count one person's pieces.
redirect_script.praise: You kept the total on top, so your fraction matches the share in the picture.

vocabulary.definition: A way to write a division: a/b means a divided by b.
The amount one person gets when a total is split equally.

next_steps.if_fail: Review grade 5 fractions as division with a sharing model (cut each whole into equal pieces and collect one person's share).

worked_example_script.text: Draw 3 rectangles for 3 sandwiches. Cut each one into 4 equal pieces. Shade one piece of each sandwich for person 1.
How many pieces does person 1 get, and what size is each piece?
Person 1 gets 3 pieces and each piece is one fourth of a sandwich, so their share is 3/4. That shows 3 divided by 4 equals 3/4.
If a student writes 4/3, ask if one person can get MORE than a whole sandwich when 4 people split only 3 sandwiches.
Your turn: 2 brownies shared by 5 kids. Draw it and write the share as a fraction.

skills.name: Divide to find a unit rate (how much per 1)

prerequisite_skill.description: Find a unit rate from a whole-number rate by dividing the total by the number of units.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: 12 dollars buys 4 pounds. How many dollars per 1 pound?

skills.i_do_script: A unit rate answers the question: how much for exactly 1? Watch: 15 dollars buys 3 pounds. I draw a double number line, pounds on top marked 0, 1, 2, 3 and dollars beneath marked 0, blank, blank, 15. To find what lines up with 1 pound, I divide the 15 dollars by the 3 pounds and get 5 dollars per 1 pound. The thing after the word per is what I divide BY, because that is the side being squeezed down to 1. The answer does not have to be a whole number: 14 dollars for 4 pounds gives 14 divided by 4, which is 3.50 per pound.

canonical_error.pattern: Divides in the wrong order, units by total instead of total by units
canonical_error.example: For '21 dollars for 6 tickets, dollars per ticket?' the student computes 6 / 21 instead of 21 / 6 = 3.50
canonical_error.why: The student divides in reading order or divides the smaller number into the larger without tracking units. The quantity being asked FOR goes on top, and the quantity after per is the divisor. A ticket that costs 29 cents should fail the sense check.

skills.item_template: A two-number whole-number rate ('A of X for B of Y') and an 'X per 1 Y' question. Whole-number or clean decimal quotients. Numeric response with occasional MC.

sample_items.stem: 20 dollars for 5 shirts. How many dollars per 1 shirt?
36 miles on 4 gallons. How many miles per 1 gallon?
45 words in 5 minutes. How many words per 1 minute?
14 dollars for 4 pounds. How many dollars per 1 pound?
6 tickets cost 21 dollars. What is the price per 1 ticket?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 15 subtracts the numbers, 126 multiplies them, 0.29 divides tickets by dollars. Only 21 / 6 = 3.50 puts dollars over tickets.

sample_items.stem: 48 students ride on 3 buses. How many students per 1 bus?
9 cups of flour makes 6 batches. How many cups per 1 batch?
60 pages print in 8 minutes. How many pages per 1 minute?

redirect_script.stop: Which quantity are you solving for, and which one comes after the word per?
redirect_script.prompt: Sketch the double number line first. The unit after per is the side you squeeze to 1, so it is what you divide BY. Say it out loud: dollars per ticket means dollars on top, tickets on the bottom. Then check the size: does your answer make sense for one?
redirect_script.praise: You put the right quantity on top before dividing, that keeps the unit rate right side up.

vocabulary.definition: How much of one quantity you get for exactly 1 of the other.
A word meaning for each 1; the quantity right after per is what you divide by.

worked_example_script.text: Draw a double number line: pounds on top marked 0, 1, 2, 3 and dollars beneath marked 0, blank, blank, 15.
The 15 dollars lines up with 3 pounds. What operation finds the dollars that line up with 1 pound?
Divide by 3. 15 divided by 3 is 5, so 5 dollars lines up with 1 pound. Dividing the total by the number of units always manufactures the 1.
If a student writes 3 / 15 = 0.2, ask whether 20 cents a pound is a sensible price when 3 pounds cost 15 dollars.
Your turn: 24 dollars for 6 hours of work. Dollars per 1 hour? Set up the division first, then compute.

practice_problems.stem: 10 dollars for 2 books. Dollars per 1 book?
18 miles in 3 hours. Miles per 1 hour?
27 dollars for 6 pizzas. Dollars per 1 pizza?
5 pounds of apples cost 12 dollars. Dollars per 1 pound?
52 dollars for 8 hours of work. Dollars per 1 hour?
9 cups of juice fills 12 glasses. Cups per 1 glass?
Which is the better buy: 3 pounds of grapes for 8.40 dollars or 5 pounds for 13.50 dollars?
practice_problems.answer: 5 pounds for 13.50: it costs 2.70 per pound, while 8.40 / 3 = 2.80 per pound.

practice_problems.stem: Kim was asked for the unit rate for '24 miles in 5 hours, miles per hour.' Find her mistake and fix it.
shown_work: unit rate is 0.2 miles per hour
practice_problems.answer: She divided hours by miles. Miles per hour puts miles on top: 24 / 5 = 4.8 miles per hour. Her 0.2 is hours per mile.

activities.title: Squeeze It to One
activities.instructions:
1. Draw a rate card like '15 dollars for 3 pounds.'
2. Build the top line in cubes: 3 pound marks. Build the bottom line: 15 cubes spread evenly under them.
3. Slide down to the 1 pound mark and count the cubes that line up under it (5).
4. Write the matching division 15 / 3 = 5 next to the line.
5. Repeat with '14 dollars for 4 pounds' and say each time: the per unit is the side we squeeze to 1.

activities.title: Per One Match-Up
materials: Card deck: one card per rate story, one card per unit rate
activities.instructions:
1. Spread the cards face up.
2. Match each rate story to its unit rate card.
3. To claim a match, say the division out loud with units: 21 dollars divided by 6 tickets is 3.50 dollars per ticket.
4. Two decoy cards show inverted divisions; set them aside and explain which unit ended up on top by mistake.

strategy_links.why: The double number line makes 'squeeze the per side to 1' visible before the divide-the-total rule is named.
Thinking aloud 'dollars per ticket, so dollars on top' models the unit tracking that prevents the inverted division.
Quick estimation talk (about how much for one?) builds the size sense that flags a 29 cent ticket as a flip.

questioning_prompts: Which quantity comes after the word per? What does that tell you to divide by?
On your double number line, which side gets squeezed to 1?
Is your answer a sensible size for ONE of that thing?
Does the unit rate have to be a whole number? Why is 3.50 fine?
If 3 pounds cost 15 dollars, what would 2 pounds cost? Does your unit rate agree?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student divides the number of units by the total, inverting the rate.
misconception_redirects.say: Read the per phrase out loud: dollars per ticket means dollars on top. Write the fraction with units before you divide, then ask if the size makes sense.
misconception_redirects.praise: You set up the fraction from the per phrase first, so the division came out right side up.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student multiplies the two numbers or subtracts them.
misconception_redirects.say: Go back to the double number line: we are sharing 21 dollars across 6 tickets, not making more dollars. Which operation shares a total equally?
misconception_redirects.praise: You recognized this as sharing, and sharing is division.

quick_checks.prompt: 35 dollars for 5 pizzas. Dollars per pizza?
14 dollars for 4 pounds. Dollars per pound?
quick_checks.look_for: 3.50, showing comfort with a non whole number unit rate.

worked_solution.stem: 6 tickets cost 21 dollars. What is the price per 1 ticket?

steps.math: per ticket, so tickets is the divisor
steps.annotation: The quantity after per is the side we squeeze to 1.
Dollars on top, tickets on the bottom.
Six 3s make 18, and the leftover 3 dollars split 6 ways is 0.50 each.
Sense check: 6 tickets at 3.50 is 21 dollars. It works.

faded_example.stem: 8 pounds of oranges cost 30 dollars. What is the price per 1 pound?

steps.math: per pound, so pounds is the divisor
steps.annotation: Pounds is the side squeezed to 1.
Dollars on top, pounds on the bottom.
Compute the division.
State the unit rate and check it by multiplying back by 8.

sentence_starters: The word per points at ___, so I divide by ___.
I divided ___ by ___ and got ___ for exactly 1 ___.

skills.name: Divide with fractions to find one share

prerequisite_skill.description: Divide a fraction by a whole number or by a fraction and interpret the quotient.

skills.i_do_script: Dividing a fraction works exactly like dividing a whole number: split it into equal shares and take one. Watch: 3/4 divided by 3. I draw a bar, shade 3/4, and see it is already 3 equal pieces of one fourth each. Splitting those 3 pieces into 3 shares gives 1 piece per share, so 3/4 divided by 3 is 1/4. When the pieces do not split evenly, I cut smaller: 1/2 divided by 7 means cutting the half into 7 slivers, and 7 slivers per half means 14 per whole, so each sliver is 1/14. The shortcut, multiply by the reciprocal, is just this cutting written fast: 1/2 x 1/7 = 1/14.

canonical_error.pattern: Multiplies by the divisor instead of its reciprocal, or flips the wrong number
canonical_error.why: The student half remembers keep change flip and flips the first fraction, or skips the flip entirely and multiplies by 7. Sharing half a mile across 7 minutes cannot give MORE than the half; the bar shows each share is a tiny sliver, 1/14.

skills.item_template: A fraction divided by a whole number, a whole number divided by a fraction, or a fraction divided by a fraction (denominators up to 12, answers clean). Numeric response.

sample_items.stem: 1/2 divided by 7
3/4 divided by 3
2/3 divided by 4
4 divided by 1/2
5/6 divided by 5
1/3 divided by 2
3 divided by 3/4
7/8 divided by 7

redirect_script.stop: Should your answer be bigger or smaller than what you started with?
redirect_script.prompt: Draw the bar first. Splitting a fraction into shares makes each share SMALLER, so dividing by a number bigger than 1 must shrink it. Flip the DIVISOR, not the first fraction, then multiply: 1/2 divided by 7 is 1/2 x 1/7.
redirect_script.praise: You flipped the divisor and your answer shrank, exactly what sharing should do.

vocabulary.definition: The flip of a number: the reciprocal of 7 is 1/7, and of 3/4 is 4/3.
The answer to a division; here, the size of one share.

worked_example_script.text: Draw a bar for one whole. Shade 3/4 of it, showing the 3 shaded fourths as separate pieces.
We need to split the shaded part into 3 equal shares. How much is one share?
The shaded 3/4 is already 3 pieces of 1/4, so each share is one piece: 3/4 divided by 3 = 1/4. The shortcut agrees: 3/4 x 1/3 = 3/12 = 1/4.
If a student answers 9/4 or 7/2 on a problem like this, point at the bar: can one share be bigger than everything we started with?
Your turn: draw 1/2 of a bar and cut it into 7 equal slivers. What fraction of the whole bar is one sliver?

practice_problems.stem: 1/2 divided by 2
1/4 divided by 3
2/5 divided by 2
3/4 divided by 6
5 divided by 1/3
2/3 divided by 1/6
A pitcher holds 2/3 cup of syrup. How many 1/4 cup servings can it fill, counting a part serving?
practice_problems.answer: 2/3 divided by 1/4 = 8/3, so 2 2/3 servings.

practice_problems.stem: Leo computed 1/2 divided by 7. Find his mistake and fix it.
practice_problems.answer: He flipped the first fraction instead of the divisor. Flip the 7: 1/2 x 1/7 = 1/14. Sharing half across 7 must give less than half, not 14.

activities.title: Share the Strip
activities.instructions:
1. Fold a strip in half and shade one half.
2. Cut the shaded half into 7 equal slivers.
3. Ask: how many slivers this size would fill the WHOLE strip? (14) So one sliver is 1/14.
4. Write the equation 1/2 divided by 7 = 1/14 next to the strip, then check it with the shortcut 1/2 x 1/7.
5. Repeat with 3/4 divided by 3 and say each time: sharing makes each piece smaller.

activities.title: Flip the Right One
materials: Worked problem slips, half correct and half with the wrong number flipped
activities.instructions:
1. Deal the slips face down.
2. Flip one at a time: decide whether the divisor was flipped or the first fraction was flipped.
3. Use the size test first: should the answer be bigger or smaller than the starting fraction?
4. Fix each wrong slip and sort into Right Flip and Wrong Flip piles; the group must agree before sorting.

content.error_step: The 1/2 was flipped instead of the 7
content.why: Only the divisor gets flipped. Dividing by 7 shares the half into 7 slivers, so the true answer 1/14 is much smaller than 1/2.

strategy_links.why: Cutting a real strip into slivers shows why dividing by 7 shrinks the fraction before keep change flip is ever named.
The flip the wrong number error is stable and predictable; sorting right flip from wrong flip work confronts it directly.
Asking bigger or smaller before computing builds the estimate that catches an answer of 14 for a sharing problem.

questioning_prompts: Before you compute: should the answer be bigger or smaller than the fraction you started with? Why?
Which number is the divisor, and which number gets flipped?
In the strip picture, how many slivers of this size fill the whole strip?
Why does dividing BY a fraction like 1/3 make the answer bigger?
How does 3/4 divided by 3 look different from 3 divided by 3/4?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student flips the first fraction or multiplies by the divisor without flipping.
misconception_redirects.say: Say the story out loud: we are SHARING 1/2 across 7. Can a share be bigger than the half? Flip only the divisor: 1/2 x 1/7.
misconception_redirects.praise: You flipped the divisor only, and your size check confirmed the answer.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student divides numerator and denominator by the whole number separately or gets lost simplifying.
misconception_redirects.say: Go back to the bar: 3/4 is 3 pieces of 1/4. Splitting 3 pieces into 3 shares is 1 piece. Let the picture do the work, then match it with the shortcut.
misconception_redirects.praise: You used the pieces in the bar to check what the shortcut said.

quick_checks.look_for: 1/6, not 2/3 or 6. The answer must be smaller than 1/3.
8, with the reasoning that there are 8 halves in 4 wholes.

steps.annotation: Sharing the half across 7 must shrink it.
Flip the divisor 7 into its reciprocal 1/7.
Multiply tops and bottoms.

steps.math: picture check: 7 slivers per half means 14 per whole
steps.annotation: Each sliver is 1/14 of the whole, matching the shortcut.
Splitting 5/6 into 5 shares shrinks it.
Flip the divisor 5 into 1/5.
Multiply tops and bottoms and simplify.
Check with the bar: 5/6 is 5 pieces of 1/6, so one share is one piece.

sentence_starters: My answer should be ___ than ___ because I am sharing it into ___ parts.
I flipped the divisor ___ into ___ and multiplied.

skills.name: Determine whether a relationship is proportional
skills.i_do_script: Before I can find a constant of proportionality, I have to know the relationship even has one. A relationship is proportional when it grows by a steady 'per 1' amount and nothing else — no fee, no head start. Watch two stories. 'A gym costs $80 per month' — proportional: 2 months is $160, the ratio 80/1 holds every time. Now 'A cleaner charges $56 per hour PLUS a $10 fee' — not proportional, because the $10 gets added no matter what, so the ratio total/hours keeps changing. My test: does it pass through zero (buy 0, pay 0) and stay the same ratio? If yes, proportional.

canonical_error.pattern: Calls any relationship with a rate 'proportional,' ignoring an added fixed fee or starting amount
canonical_error.example: Marks 'A taxi charges $3 plus $2 per mile' as proportional because it has a per-mile rate
canonical_error.why: The student keys on the presence of a rate word ('per mile') and stops, not testing whether the relationship passes through the origin. The fixed $3 means 0 miles still costs $3, so the ratio cost/miles is not constant — it is not proportional.

skills.item_template: Four verbal descriptions (or tables); exactly one is proportional (pure rate, through origin), the rest carry a fixed fee / deposit / head start. Student selects the proportional one. MC with 4 choices.

sample_items.stem: Choose the description that represents a proportional relationship.
sample_items.answer: A gym membership costs $80 per month.
choices: A cleaning company charges $56 per hour plus a $10 service fee.
A gym membership costs $80 per month.
A man pays a $50 deposit and $20 per hour to rent a car.
A student orders two pizzas and pays a delivery fee.
sample_items.distractor_logic: The three distractors each add a fixed amount (fee, deposit, delivery) on top of a rate, so they do not pass through the origin; only the gym membership is a pure rate.

sample_items.stem: Which table represents a proportional relationship?
sample_items.distractor_logic: B and D have a constant difference but not a constant ratio; C does not pass through (0,0); only A keeps y/x = 4 for every row.

sample_items.stem: A relationship passes through the point (0, 5) on a graph and rises steadily. Is it proportional?
sample_items.answer: No — a proportional graph must pass through the origin (0, 0); this one starts at 5.
choices: Yes, because it rises at a steady rate.
No — a proportional graph must pass through the origin (0, 0); this one starts at 5.
Yes, because it is a straight line.
sample_items.distractor_logic: A and C reward 'straight and steady' without checking the origin; a line through (0,5) is linear but not proportional.

sample_items.stem: Which statement describes a proportional relationship between distance and time?
sample_items.answer: A runner keeps a steady 6 miles per hour from a standing start.
choices: A runner gets a 2-mile head start, then runs 6 miles per hour.
A runner keeps a steady 6 miles per hour from a standing start.
A runner speeds up a little every minute.
A runner stops to rest halfway.
sample_items.distractor_logic: The head start breaks the origin; speeding up breaks the constant ratio; resting breaks steadiness. Only the steady-from-zero runner is proportional.

redirect_script.stop: Wait — what does it cost when you buy zero?
redirect_script.prompt: Test the origin. Ask 'if I buy 0 or wait 0 hours, is the total 0?' If there's a fee or head start hiding in the words, the answer isn't 0 — so it is NOT proportional.
redirect_script.praise: You caught the hidden fee — checking the zero point is exactly how you spot a fake.

vocabulary.definition: A relationship where y is always the same constant times x, so the graph passes through (0, 0).
The point (0, 0); a proportional relationship must pass through it.
The value y/x is the same for every pair in the relationship.

worked_example_script.text: Write two stories side by side: (A) 'Apples cost $2 per pound.' (B) 'A booth charges $5 to enter, then $2 per pound of apples.'
In each story, what do you pay if you buy 0 pounds?
Story A: 0 pounds costs $0 — it passes through the origin. Story B: 0 pounds still costs $5 — the entry fee. That fee is what breaks proportionality.
Check the ratio too. In A, 2/1, 4/2, 6/3 are all 2. In B, is 7/1 the same as 9/2?
If a student calls B proportional 'because it has a per-pound rate,' point only to the 0-pound cost — let the $5 give it away.
Your turn: 'A phone plan is $30 per month.' Proportional? What does 0 months cost?

practice_problems.stem: A table shows (1, 5), (2, 10), (3, 15). Is y/x the same every row? Is it proportional?
practice_problems.answer: Yes — y/x = 5 every row, and it passes through (0,0).

practice_problems.stem: Fill in the blank: a proportional graph always passes through the point ____.
practice_problems.answer: (0, 0), the origin

practice_problems.stem: 'A rideshare charges a $4 pickup fee plus $2 per mile.' Proportional or not? How do you know?
practice_problems.answer: Not proportional — 0 miles still costs $4, so it does not pass through the origin.
practice_problems.notes: Baits the canonical error: a rate word is present but a fee breaks the origin.

practice_problems.stem: Which is proportional? (A) y = 3x   (B) y = 3x + 2
practice_problems.answer: A. y = 3x passes through (0,0); y = 3x + 2 starts at 2.
practice_problems.notes: First look at proportional vs non-proportional in equation form; the +2 is the fee in disguise.

practice_problems.stem: Priya was asked which relationship is proportional. Find her mistake and fix it.
shown_work: The choices were: (a) $6 per hour, (b) $10 sign-up plus $6 per hour.
Priya wrote: 'Both have $6 per hour, so both are proportional.'
practice_problems.answer: Only (a) is proportional. Choice (b) adds a fixed $10 sign-up fee, so 0 hours still costs $10 — it does not pass through the origin. A per-hour rate alone is not enough.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error with fresh numbers: 'has a rate, therefore proportional.'

practice_problems.stem: A table shows (2, 6), (4, 12), (5, 14). Is it proportional?
practice_problems.answer: No — 6/2 = 3 and 12/4 = 3, but 14/5 = 2.8. The ratio is not constant.
practice_problems.notes: Two rows agree, the third betrays it — students must check every row.

practice_problems.stem: Write one proportional and one non-proportional story about the cost of buying pencils. Explain what makes each one what it is.
practice_problems.answer: Sample: proportional — 'pencils cost $0.25 each' (0 pencils, $0). Non-proportional — 'a $1 box plus $0.25 per pencil' (0 pencils still $1).
practice_problems.notes: Reversed direction — produce and justify both, not just recognize.

practice_problems.stem: A graph is a straight line through (0, 0). A classmate says 'straight lines are always proportional.' Are they right?
practice_problems.answer: Not always — a straight line is proportional only if it passes through the origin. A line through (0, 3) is straight but not proportional. This one is proportional because it goes through (0,0).
practice_problems.notes: Separates 'linear' from 'proportional' — the classic over-generalization.

activities.title: Origin or Not: Proportional Sort
materials: Card set of 12 rate stories/tables (6 proportional, 6 with a hidden fee or head start)
activities.instructions:
1. Spread all 12 cards face up.
2. Sort into two piles: 'Proportional' and 'Not proportional.'
3. Rule to place a card: say out loud what it costs (or where it is) at zero. If zero gives zero, it's proportional.
4. For any 'not proportional' card, circle the exact word that adds a fee or head start.
5. Debrief: what did every non-proportional card have in common?

cards.text: $5 per hour plus a $12 flat fee

activities.title: The Rate-Word Trap
activities.instructions:
1. Students read Priya's claim that both '$6 per hour' and '$10 sign-up plus $6 per hour' are proportional.
2. They write what Priya noticed correctly (both have a rate) and exactly what she skipped (the origin test).

4. Share out: why isn't 'has a per-hour rate' enough to call something proportional?

content.worked_problem: Which is proportional? (a) $6 per hour, (b) $10 sign-up plus $6 per hour. Priya says both.

activities.title: Zero Check Lightning Round
materials: Slide deck or index cards of rate stories
activities.instructions:

skills.name: Identify the constant of proportionality when the pair (1, r) is shown
skills.i_do_script: Think of each price tag as dollars spread over a row of pound-blocks. The question 'dollars per 1 pound' is asking about a picture with exactly ONE pound-block -- not about a picture that happens to have a $1 bill in it somewhere. The easiest place to find the constant of proportionality is when the relationship hands you the pair with a 1 in it. In a table, if a row says (1, 5), then k is 5 — five y for one x, done. In a list of rate statements, the one that already uses 'per 1' or shows 1 of something is the unit rate. Watch four statements: '$2 for 1 apple,' '$5 for 2 apples,' '$7 for 3 apples,' '$1 for 5 apples.' Only the first pairs with exactly 1, so its number, $2, is the unit rate.

canonical_error.pattern: Picks the statement or row with the smallest total, or the largest quantity, instead of the one paired with 1
canonical_error.example: Chooses '$1 for 5 apples' as the unit rate because '$1' looks like a unit, instead of '$2 for 1 apple'
canonical_error.why: The student anchors on the numeral 1 wherever it appears — often the price — rather than requiring the QUANTITY (the second value) to be 1. A unit rate needs the 1 attached to the thing you are measuring per.

skills.item_template: Four rate statements or a short table; exactly one pairs the second quantity with 1. Student selects the unit rate / constant. MC with 4 choices.

sample_items.stem: Which statement represents a unit rate?
sample_items.distractor_logic: $5/2, $7/3 pair with more than one apple; '$1 for 5 apples' baits the student who grabs the numeral 1 from the price. Only '$2 for 1 apple' pairs the quantity with 1.

sample_items.stem: A table of a proportional relationship includes the row (1, 9). What is the constant of proportionality?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 1 grabs the x-value; 10 adds the pair; 1/9 inverts the ratio. When x = 1, k is simply the y-value, 9.

sample_items.stem: A graph of a proportional relationship passes through (1, 4). What is the unit rate?
sample_items.distractor_logic: The point (1, 4) hands over the unit rate directly: 4 y for 1 x. Distractors grab the x, sum the pair, or invert.

sample_items.stem: Which rate is the unit rate for miles per gallon?
sample_items.distractor_logic: '1 mile for 24 gallons' baits the numeral-1 grab but pairs 1 with the wrong quantity; only '24 miles for 1 gallon' has 1 gallon as the unit.

redirect_script.stop: Which of your numbers is the amount, and is IT a 1?
redirect_script.prompt: Sketch the choice as pound-blocks first: how many blocks are in your picture? The unit rate pairs with 1 of the thing you measure per — usually the SECOND quantity. Point to the second number in each choice; keep only the choice where that number is 1.
redirect_script.praise: You made the quantity — not just any 1 — equal to one. That's the real unit rate.

vocabulary.definition: The amount of the first quantity for exactly 1 of the second quantity.
A table row or graph point where x = 1; its y-value is the constant of proportionality.

worked_example_script.text: Sketch two of the choices as pound-blocks: '$3 for 1 pound' is a single block carrying all $3; '$1 for 4 pounds' is FOUR blocks sharing one dollar between them.
Which sketch has exactly ONE pound-block? In the four-block sketch, how much does each single block get -- is it $1?

Only '$3 for 1 pound' is a one-block picture, so the unit rate is $3. In the other sketch the $1 is smeared across 4 blocks -- each pound gets just 25 cents. The 1 has to be on the POUNDS, not the price.
List: '$3 for 1 pound,' '$8 for 3 pounds,' '$1 for 4 pounds,' '$6 for 2 pounds.'
We want dollars per 1 POUND. Which choice has exactly 1 pound?
If a student picks '$1 for 4 pounds' because of the $1, ask 'is the POUND number a 1 there? What is it?'
Only '$3 for 1 pound' pairs with 1 pound, so the unit rate is $3. The $1 in the trap answer is dollars, not pounds.
Your turn: a table row reads (1, 12). What is k? Where did you look?

practice_problems.notes: Directs attention to the (1, r) row rather than dividing.

practice_problems.stem: Marcus was asked for the unit rate. Find and fix his mistake.
shown_work: Choices: '$4 for 1 yard,' '$9 for 3 yards,' '$1 for 6 yards.'
Marcus chose '$1 for 6 yards' and wrote 'the unit rate is $1 because it has a 1.'
practice_problems.answer: The 1 has to be on the YARDS (the quantity we measure per), not on the dollars. '$1 for 6 yards' pairs 1 with dollars. The correct unit rate is '$4 for 1 yard,' so k = 4.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: grabbing the numeral 1 from the wrong quantity.

practice_problems.stem: A graph passes through (1, 2.5). What is the constant of proportionality?
practice_problems.notes: The (1, r) value can be a decimal — still read directly.

practice_problems.notes: Marks the boundary of this skill and sets up S3 (compute).

practice_problems.stem: Write a table for a proportional relationship whose constant of proportionality is 6, and include the row that shows it at a glance.
practice_problems.answer: Sample: (1, 6), (2, 12), (3, 18). The (1, 6) row shows k = 6 directly.

materials: Card set: 6 mini rate-lists, each with one true unit-rate card and three decoys

materials: Card set of 12 rate statements (6 pair with 1, 6 pair with 2+ )
activities.instructions:
1. Sort every card into 'Unit rate' (pairs with exactly 1) or 'Not yet a unit rate.'
2. For each 'not yet' card, write what you'd divide by to fix it.
3. Trade piles with another group and check.
4. Debrief: a unit rate isn't the smallest number — it's the one attached to 1.

strategy_links.why: The core failure is picking a decoy 1; comparing the true (1, r) pair against numeral-1 traps is targeted error analysis.

questioning_prompts: Which quantity are we measuring 'per'? Is THAT number a 1?
In a table, which row hands you k without any dividing?
This choice has a 1 in it — a 1 of what?
If a graph goes through (1, r), what is k?
Is the smallest price always the unit rate? Why not?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student picks the option with a 1 in the price (or the smallest number) instead of the one paired with 1 unit of the quantity.
misconception_redirects.say: The unit rate pairs with 1 of the thing you measure per — usually the SECOND quantity. Point to the second number in each choice; keep only the choice where that number is 1.
misconception_redirects.praise: You made the quantity — not just any 1 — equal to one. That's the real unit rate.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student reads (1, r) and reports the x-value (1) as the constant.
misconception_redirects.say: When x is 1, the constant is the OTHER number — the y. The 1 is just telling you you're looking at the right row.
misconception_redirects.praise: You read the y-value at x = 1 — that's the constant of proportionality.

quick_checks.prompt: Which is the unit rate: '$6 for 2 pens' or '$3 for 1 pen'?
quick_checks.look_for: '$3 for 1 pen.' Choosing '$6 for 2' means the student isn't requiring the quantity to be 1.

quick_checks.prompt: A table row says (1, 8). What is k?
quick_checks.look_for: 8. An answer of 1 means the student read the x instead of the y.

At x = 1 the y-value is ___, so k = ___.

steps.annotation: The constant is easiest to read where x is exactly 1.
No dividing needed — the y at x = 1 IS the constant.
Every row gives the same k, confirming 7.
Seven y for one x.

steps.math: look for the row where x = 1
steps.annotation: That row hands over k directly.
The y-value here is the constant.
Write the constant of proportionality (the y at x = 1).
Check it against another row: is 36/3 the same?

skills.name: Calculate the constant of proportionality as y divided by x
skills.i_do_script: Most of the time the relationship will NOT hand you a 1 -- you have to make one, and a double number line shows what the division is doing. A runner goes 17 miles in 2 hours: draw hours on top (0, 1, 2) and miles beneath (0, ?, 17). The unit rate is whatever lines up with 1 hour -- halfway, 8.5 miles. Dividing y by x IS that move: it shrinks the pair (17, 2) down to the pair (8.5, 1). It works for any pair, any numbers: 93 words in 4 minutes gives 93/4 = 23.25 words per minute -- not a whole number, and that's fine. The setup habit: the unit after 'per' is the one you squeeze to 1, so it goes on the bottom.

canonical_error.pattern: Divides x by y (input by output) instead of y by x, inverting the constant
canonical_error.example: For '93 words in 4 minutes, words per minute?' the student computes 4 / 93 instead of 93 / 4
canonical_error.why: The student divides the smaller number into the larger out of habit, or follows reading order, without tracking that the unit rate they want (words per minute) puts words on top. Inverting gives minutes per word, a different quantity.

skills.item_template: A verbal description or table pair with no (1, r) row; whole numbers that produce a non-whole unit rate. Student computes k = y/x. Numeric response.

sample_items.stem: A student writes 93 words in 4 minutes. What is the unit rate, in words per minute?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Inverting gives 4/93; forgetting the remainder gives 23. The correct k = 93 / 4 = 23.25.

sample_items.stem: A car travels 130 miles on 4 gallons of gas. What is the unit rate, in miles per gallon?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 130/4 = 32.5; the trap 4/130 gives gallons per mile.

sample_items.stem: A table row of a proportional relationship is (6, 27). What is the constant of proportionality?
A printer produces 50 pages in 8 minutes. What is the unit rate, in pages per minute?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 50/8 = 6.25 pages per minute; 8/50 gives minutes per page.

redirect_script.stop: Which unit should end up on top?
redirect_script.prompt: Sketch the double number line: which side must shrink to 1? What lines up with it? Read the 'per' phrase — 'words per minute' means words on top. Write the fraction words over minutes, THEN divide. If your answer is a tiny decimal below 1, you flipped it.
redirect_script.praise: You put the output on top and divided — that's the constant of proportionality, decimal and all.

vocabulary.definition: The value k = y/x, the same for every pair in a proportional relationship.
The quantity you are measuring per 1 — it goes on top when you divide.
The 'per' quantity — it goes on the bottom (you divide by it).

worked_example_script.text: Draw a double number line: hours on top marked 0, 1, 2; miles beneath marked 0, ?, 17.
The 17 miles lines up with 2 hours. What lines up with 1 hour -- and what operation finds it?
Half of 17 -- dividing by 2 slides the pair down to (8.5, 1). Dividing y by x always manufactures the 1; 'per hour' tells you hours is the side being squeezed to 1.
Write 'A runner goes 17 miles in 2 hours. Miles per hour?'
The phrase 'miles per hour' — which unit goes on top?
Miles on top, hours on the bottom: 17 over 2. Now divide: 17 divided by 2 is 8.5 miles per hour.
If a student writes 2/17 = 0.12, ask 'does one-tenth of a mile an hour make sense for a runner? Which unit did you put on top?'
Your turn: 45 dollars for 6 hours of work. Dollars per hour? Set up the fraction first, then divide.

practice_problems.stem: A table row is (2, 9). What is y divided by x?
For 'miles per gallon,' which quantity goes on top before you divide?
practice_problems.answer: Miles (the output).

practice_problems.answer: Lena divided hours by miles. 'Miles per hour' needs miles on top: 78 / 5 = 15.6 miles per hour. Her 0.064 is hours per mile — the flipped quantity.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: inverting the division.

practice_problems.stem: A recipe uses 25 grams of cocoa for 4 servings. Grams per serving?
practice_problems.notes: Bakes in a non-whole k.

practice_problems.stem: Two pay rates: $95 for 8 hours, or $70 for 6 hours. Which is the higher unit rate?

practice_problems.notes: Comparing forces two correct divisions and guards against comparing raw totals.

practice_problems.stem: A unit rate came out to exactly 12.5 dollars per hour. Write one pair of whole numbers (dollars, hours) that produces it.
practice_problems.answer: Sample: $25 for 2 hours (25 / 2 = 12.5), or $50 for 4 hours.
practice_problems.notes: Reversed direction — build a pair from the constant.

activities.title: Top-or-Bottom Setup Station
activities.instructions:
1. Draw a rate-story card ('84 beats in 5 seconds, beats per second?').
2. Before any dividing, place the two numbers into the TOP and BOTTOM trays using the 'per' phrase.
3. Only then write the division on the whiteboard and compute.
4. Check: if the answer is less than 1 and that seems wrong for the story, you swapped the trays.
5. Debrief: how does the 'per' phrase decide the top every time?

activities.title: Flip Detector
activities.instructions:
1. Read Lena's claim that the unit rate is 0.064 miles per hour.
2. Decide whether her answer is too big or too small for the story, and say how you know.
3. Redo the division with the right unit on top.
4. Write one sentence: how can a quick 'does this size make sense?' check catch a flip?

content.worked_problem: 78 miles in 5 hours. Miles per hour? Lena wrote 5 / 78 = 0.064.
content.error_step: Lena divided hours by miles instead of miles by hours.
content.why: 'Miles per hour' puts miles on top: 78 / 5 = 15.6. Her answer is hours per mile.

strategy_links.why: Physically placing numbers into TOP/BOTTOM trays before dividing is the representational bridge to the abstract y/x rule.
Thinking aloud 'miles per hour, so miles on top' models the unit-tracking that prevents the inversion error.
Number-talk estimation ('about how many miles per hour?') builds the size-sense that flags a flipped answer.

Is your answer a sensible size for this story? Bigger or smaller than 1?
Does the constant have to be a whole number? Why is a decimal okay here?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student divides input by output (x by y), producing the reciprocal.
misconception_redirects.say: Read the 'per' phrase — 'words per minute' means words on top. Write the fraction words over minutes, THEN divide. If your answer is a tiny decimal below 1, you flipped it.

y divided by x is ___ / ___ = ___, the constant of proportionality.

skills.name: Find a unit rate when the quantities are fractions
skills.i_do_script: The rule doesn't change when fractions show up -- it's still y divided by x -- but picture what the division does: the amount gets shared across the time. A bus travels 1/2 mile in 7 minutes: that half mile is spread over 7 minutes, so each single minute gets a seventh of the half -- 1/2 divided by 7 = 1/2 x 1/7 = 1/14 mile per minute. Estimate BEFORE computing: 7 minutes for half a mile is slow, so the per-minute rate must be much smaller than 1/2 -- and 1/14 is. If your answer comes out bigger than the amount you started with, the division was probably upside down.

canonical_error.pattern: Divides the whole number by the fraction (or ignores the fraction), instead of the fraction by the whole number
canonical_error.example: For '1/2 mile in 7 minutes, miles per minute?' the student computes 7 divided by 1/2 = 14, or just 1/2 divided into 7 backwards
canonical_error.why: The student wants the bigger number involved in a way that yields a 'nicer' answer, and reverses the division. Miles per minute must be (miles) / (minutes) = (1/2) / 7, which is much less than 1.

skills.item_template: A fractional quantity over a whole-number quantity (or vice versa) with a 'per' question. Student computes k by dividing a fraction. Numeric response as a fraction.

sample_items.stem: A city bus travels 1/2 of a mile in 7 minutes. What is the unit rate, in miles per minute?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 1/2 divided by 7 = 1/14; the trap 7 / (1/2) = 14 inverts the setup.

sample_items.stem: A snail crawls 3/4 of a foot in 6 seconds. What is the unit rate, in feet per second?
A painter uses 2/3 of a gallon in 4 hours. What is the unit rate, in gallons per hour?
sample_items.distractor_logic: (2/3) / 4 = 2/12 = 1/6; multiplying instead of dividing gives 8/3.

sample_items.stem: A reader finishes 3/5 of a chapter in 9 minutes. What is the unit rate, in chapters per minute?
sample_items.distractor_logic: (3/5) / 9 = 3/45 = 1/15; the flipped setup 9 / (3/5) = 15 is the bait.

redirect_script.stop: Which number is the miles, and which is the minutes?
redirect_script.prompt: Estimate first: the amount is being SHARED across the time, so the per-unit rate must be smaller than the amount. Miles per minute means miles on top — that's the FRACTION, 1/2. Minutes is on the bottom, so you divide 1/2 by 7. Dividing by 7 is timesing by 1/7.
redirect_script.praise: You divided the fraction by the whole number and kept the units straight — that's a real fractional unit rate.

vocabulary.definition: The flip of a number; dividing by 7 is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal, 1/7.
A fraction whose top or bottom is itself a fraction, like (1/2) over 7 — it means (1/2) divided by 7.

worked_example_script.text: Draw a 1-mile bar. Shade the 1/2 mile traveled, then cut that half into 7 equal shares -- one share per minute.

visual.label: The 1/2 mile is 7 shares of the mile's 14ths -- each minute gets one share

worked_example_script.text: Before any computing: will the per-minute distance be bigger or smaller than 1/2? A lot smaller or a little?
Write 'A tap drips 1/3 of a cup in 5 minutes. Cups per minute?'
'Cups per minute' — which quantity goes on top? Is it a whole number or a fraction?
Cups on top: that's 1/3. Minutes on the bottom: 5. So we divide 1/3 by 5, which is 1/3 times 1/5 = 1/15 cup per minute.
If a student writes 5 divided by 1/3 = 15, ask 'is your answer bigger or smaller than 1 cup? Can one minute really give 15 cups from a slow drip?'

activities.title: Size-Sense Check
activities.instructions:
1. Read Theo's claim of 24 miles per minute for a trip of 1/4 mile in 6 minutes.
2. Without computing, decide: should the answer be bigger or smaller than 1? Why?
3. Redo the division correctly (fraction on top).
4. Write the rule you'd tell Theo so he never makes this flip again.

content.worked_problem: 1/4 mile in 6 minutes. Miles per minute? Theo wrote 6 / (1/4) = 24.
content.error_step: Theo divided minutes by miles, and by the fraction rather than by the whole number.
content.why: Miles per minute is (1/4) / 6 = 1/24. Traveling only a quarter mile in 6 minutes must be far less than 1 mile per minute.

strategy_links.why: Fraction bars or a number line make 'a fraction split into equal minutes' concrete before the reciprocal rule.
Inverted answers (14 instead of 1/14) are the signature error; matching correct rates against flipped decoys targets it.
Thinking aloud about the SIZE of the answer ('a quarter mile in 6 minutes must be tiny') models the estimate that catches inversion.

questioning_prompts: Which quantity is the fraction — and does it belong on top or bottom?
Dividing by a whole number is the same as multiplying by what?
Should this unit rate be bigger or smaller than 1? How do you know before computing?
Where did the whole number go — did you divide BY it or INTO it?
Why does a small distance over many minutes give a tiny unit rate?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student divides the whole number by the fraction (7 / (1/2) = 14) and reports a large unit rate.
misconception_redirects.say: Miles per minute means miles on top — that's the FRACTION, 1/2. Minutes is on the bottom, so you divide 1/2 by 7. Dividing by 7 is timesing by 1/7.
misconception_redirects.praise: You divided the fraction by the whole number and kept the units straight — that's a real fractional unit rate.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student sets up (1/2) / 7 correctly but multiplies by 7 instead of by 1/7.
misconception_redirects.say: To divide by 7, flip it to 1/7 and multiply. So 1/2 times 1/7, not 1/2 times 7.
misconception_redirects.praise: You used the reciprocal — divide by 7 becomes times one-seventh.

quick_checks.prompt: 1/2 mile in 4 minutes. Miles per minute?
quick_checks.look_for: 1/8. An answer of 8 diagnoses dividing the whole number by the fraction.

quick_checks.prompt: Should the unit rate for '1/3 gallon in 9 minutes' be more or less than 1 gallon per minute?
quick_checks.look_for: Less than 1 (it's 1/27). 'More than 1' means the student expects a large answer and will invert.

sentence_starters: The fraction ___ goes on top, divided by ___, so I multiply by the reciprocal ___.
Because the distance is small over many units, the unit rate should be ___ than 1.

worked_solution.stem: A leaky faucet loses 2/3 of a liter in 8 minutes. What is the unit rate, in liters per minute?

steps.math: 'liters per minute' -> liters (2/3) on top, minutes (8) on bottom
steps.annotation: Set up y/x with the fraction as the output.
Dividing by 8 is multiplying by its reciprocal, 1/8.
Multiply straight across, then simplify.
Less than 1 — sensible for a slow leak.

faded_example.stem: A glacier moves 3/4 of a meter in 9 days. What is the unit rate, in meters per day?

steps.math: meters (3/4) on top, days (9) on bottom
steps.annotation: Output over input.
Divide by 9 = multiply by 1/9.
Multiply across and simplify the fraction.
State k; check that it is less than 1 for this slow motion.

skills.name: Identify the constant of proportionality from an equation or a graph
skills.i_do_script: One test unmasks k in any costume: feed in x = 1. In y = 6x, one x gives y = 6; in y = x/2, one x gives y = 1/2 -- not 2. Whatever y pops out at x = 1 is the constant, no matter which number is biggest on the page. Two representations give up the constant almost for free once you know where to look. In an equation written as y = kx, the constant is the number multiplying x — nothing to compute. In y = 4x, k is 4. On a graph of a proportional line, the constant is the y-value at x = 1 — find where the line crosses the vertical gridline above 1, and read straight up. Both are just 'where does k hide in THIS costume.'

canonical_error.pattern: In an equation, reads a number that is added or is the y-variable as k; on a graph, reads a convenient point instead of the value at x = 1
canonical_error.example: For y = x/4 the student says k = 4 instead of 1/4; or on a graph through (2, 6) and (1, 3), reports k = 6 (from the point (2,6)) instead of 3
canonical_error.why: The student pattern-matches on the biggest or first number rather than the structure. In y = kx, k multiplies x (so y = x/4 means k = 1/4). On a graph, only the value paired with x = 1 is the constant; any other point must be divided.

skills.item_template: An equation in the form y = kx (including y = x/n) or a described/plotted proportional line. Student states k. MC or numeric response.

sample_items.stem: What is the constant of proportionality for y = 8x?
sample_items.distractor_logic: k is the coefficient of x. 1 grabs the implied 1 on y; 1/8 inverts; 9 adds.

sample_items.stem: What is the constant of proportionality for y = x/4?
sample_items.distractor_logic: y = x/4 is y = (1/4)x, so k = 1/4. '4' is the classic trap of reading the visible number.

sample_items.stem: A proportional line passes through (1, 5) and (3, 15). What is the constant of proportionality?
sample_items.distractor_logic: The value at x = 1 is 5, so k = 5. '15' reads the point (3,15) without dividing; '3' grabs an x-value.

sample_items.stem: A proportional graph passes through the origin and the point (4, 10). What is the unit rate?
sample_items.distractor_logic: No (1, r) point is shown, so divide: 10/4 = 2.5. '10' reads the point raw; '0.4' inverts.

redirect_script.stop: In y = kx, which number multiplies the x?
redirect_script.prompt: Run the x = 1 test first: when x is exactly 1, what y does your equation (or your line) actually give? Circle the number stuck to the x — that's k. If the equation is y = x/4, rewrite it as y = (1/4)x first. On a graph, only the point above 1 gives k directly; for any other point, divide y by x.
redirect_script.praise: You read the multiplier of x — that's the constant, no computing needed.

vocabulary.definition: The number multiplied by a variable; in y = kx the coefficient of x is the constant k.
The equation form of every proportional relationship; k is the constant of proportionality.

worked_example_script.text: Plug x = 1 into y = 6x. What y comes out? Now plug x = 1 into y = x/2 -- what y comes out this time?
y = 6 and y = 1/2. The output at x = 1 IS the constant: k = 6 for the first, k = 1/2 for the second -- even though the 2 is the number you SEE on the page.
On a graph, run the same test with your finger: slide to x = 1 and read the height. The line through (0, 0) and (1, 3) stands at height 3 above x = 1, so its k is 3.
Write two equations: y = 6x and y = x/2.
In y = 6x, what number is multiplying the x? That's k.
k = 6. Now y = x/2 is sneaky — dividing by 2 is the same as multiplying by 1/2, so y = (1/2)x and k = 1/2, not 2.
Sketch a proportional line through (0,0) and (1, 3); mark the vertical line at x = 1.
If a student reads a random point like (2, 6) and says k = 6, ask 'what x does that go with? Where is x exactly 1?'
Your turn: y = x/5, and a line through (1, 4). Give k for each.

practice_problems.stem: What is k in y = 12x?
On a proportional graph, the constant is the y-value at x = ____.
What is k in y = x/3?
practice_problems.answer: 1/3 (because y = (1/3)x)
practice_problems.notes: Baits the 'read the 3' error.

practice_problems.stem: A proportional line passes through (1, 7). What is the constant of proportionality?
practice_problems.notes: Value at x = 1 read directly.

practice_problems.stem: Ava was asked for the constant of proportionality of y = x/6. Find and fix her mistake.
shown_work: Ava wrote: 'The number I see is 6, so k = 6.'
practice_problems.answer: y = x/6 means y = (1/6)x, so k = 1/6. Dividing x by 6 is multiplying by 1/6 — the constant is the multiplier of x, not the number you happen to see.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: reading the visible number instead of the coefficient.

practice_problems.stem: A proportional graph passes through (2, 9). What is k?
practice_problems.answer: 4.5 (9 / 2, since x is not 1)
practice_problems.notes: Point isn't at x = 1, so divide.

practice_problems.stem: Line A is y = 3x. Line B passes through (1, 5). Which has the greater constant of proportionality?
practice_problems.answer: Line B — k = 5 (from the point at x = 1) beats Line A's k = 3.
practice_problems.notes: Compares k across two representations.

practice_problems.stem: Write an equation in the form y = kx whose constant is 2/3, and give the point it passes through at x = 1.
practice_problems.answer: y = (2/3)x, passing through (1, 2/3).
practice_problems.notes: Reversed direction — build the equation and its (1, r) point from k.

activities.title: Where's k? Across Representations
materials: Card set mixing equations (y = kx, y = x/n) and described graph points
activities.instructions:
1. Each card shows a proportional relationship as either an equation or a point on a graph.
2. Sort cards by their constant of proportionality (group all the 'k = 1/2' cards together, etc.).
3. For each equation like y = x/4, rewrite it as y = (1/4)x on the card before sorting.
4. For each graph point not at x = 1, write the division you used.
5. Debrief: how do you find k in an equation vs on a graph?

activities.title: The Number I See Trap
materials: Slip with Ava's y = x/6 work
activities.instructions:
1. Read Ava's claim that k = 6 for y = x/6.
2. Rewrite the equation so the constant is easy to see.
3. State the correct k and explain why dividing by 6 makes the constant 1/6.
4. Write one sentence Ava can memorize about where k lives in y = kx.

content.error_step: Ava read the visible 6 instead of the coefficient of x.
content.why: y = x/6 is y = (1/6)x, so the multiplier of x is 1/6. The constant is 1/6, not 6.

strategy_links.why: The y = x/n trap and the wrong-point-on-a-graph trap are precise, baitable errors that error analysis exposes.
Thinking aloud 'the constant multiplies x, so I rewrite x/6 as (1/6)x' models the structural read this skill needs.
Gradual release across three representations (equation, then graph, then mixed) scaffolds the transfer of 'find k' between costumes.

questioning_prompts: In y = kx, which number is stuck to the x?
How do you rewrite y = x/4 so the constant is obvious?
On this graph, where is x exactly 1? What's the y there?
This point isn't at x = 1 — what do you do instead?
Same relationship, an equation and a graph — do they give the same k?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student reports the visible number in y = x/n as k (says k = 4 for y = x/4), or reads a non-(1,r) graph point raw.
misconception_redirects.say: Circle the number stuck to the x — that's k. If the equation is y = x/4, rewrite it as y = (1/4)x first. On a graph, only the point above 1 gives k directly; for any other point, divide y by x.
misconception_redirects.praise: You read the multiplier of x — that's the constant, no computing needed.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student reads a graph point like (4, 10) and reports k = 10 without dividing.
misconception_redirects.say: That point is at x = 4, not 1. Divide the y by the x — 10 divided by 4 — to get the per-1 value.
misconception_redirects.praise: You scaled the point down to x = 1 instead of reading it raw — that's the constant.

quick_checks.prompt: What is k in y = x/5?
quick_checks.look_for: 1/5. An answer of 5 diagnoses reading the visible number rather than the coefficient.

quick_checks.prompt: A proportional line passes through (2, 7). What is k?
quick_checks.look_for: 3.5. An answer of 7 means the student read the point without scaling to x = 1.

sentence_starters: In y = kx the number multiplying x is ___, so k = ___.
The point above x = 1 is ___, so the constant is ___.

worked_solution.stem: A proportional relationship is written as y = x/8. What is the constant of proportionality, and what point does the graph pass through at x = 1?

steps.annotation: Dividing x by 8 is multiplying by 1/8 — this exposes k.
In y = kx, k is whatever multiplies x.
The graph crosses x = 1 at height 1/8 — the same constant.
Equation and graph agree.

faded_example.stem: A proportional relationship is written as y = x/10. What is the constant of proportionality, and what point does the graph pass through at x = 1?

steps.annotation: Turn 'divide by 10' into a multiplier.

steps.math: the multiplier of x is the constant
steps.annotation: Read k as the coefficient of x.
State k.
Find the y at x = 1 to give the point (1, ___).

skills.name: Interpret the constant of proportionality and use it to predict
skills.i_do_script: Finding k is only worth it if you can USE it. Once I have the constant, the whole relationship is y = kx, and I can predict any value. Watch: granola costs $2.80 for 7 ounces, so k = 2.80 / 7 = $0.40 per ounce, and the equation is c = 0.40w. Now I can answer a question the table never listed: 26 ounces costs 0.40 times 26 = $10.40. The constant is the engine; the equation lets me drive it anywhere.

canonical_error.pattern: Finds k correctly but then adds or scales incorrectly when predicting, or multiplies by the wrong quantity
canonical_error.example: With k = 0.40 per ounce, to find the cost of 26 ounces the student computes 0.40 + 26 or uses the original 7 ounces again instead of 0.40 x 26
canonical_error.why: The student treats the prediction as a fresh, disconnected step and loses the structure y = kx. Prediction is always multiply the constant by the NEW input; any adding, or reusing the old numbers, breaks the proportional model.

skills.item_template: A proportional context; student finds k, writes/uses y = kx, and predicts a value for a new input. Multi-part (identify equation + compute a prediction). Numeric response.

sample_items.stem:
The cost of granola is proportional to its weight. Granola costs $2.80 for 7 ounces.

Part A: Write the equation relating cost c and weight w.
Part B: What is the cost of 26 ounces?
sample_items.distractor_logic: k = 2.80/7 = 0.40 gives c = 0.40w; Part B is 0.40 x 26 = 10.40. Adding (0.40 + 26) or reusing 7 oz are the traps.

sample_items.stem:
A car travels at a constant speed and covers 120 miles in 3 hours.

Part A: What is the constant of proportionality (miles per hour)?
Part B: How far does it travel in 7 hours?
sample_items.distractor_logic: k = 120/3 = 40; distance = 40 x 7 = 280. Reusing 3 hours or adding gives wrong results.

sample_items.stem:
Ribbon costs a constant rate; 5 feet costs $3.75.

Part A: Write the equation for cost c and length f.
Part B: What does 12 feet cost?

A recipe scales proportionally: 4 servings use 6 cups of broth.

Part A: Cups per serving?
Part B: How many cups for 10 servings?
sample_items.distractor_logic: k = 6/4 = 1.5 cups per serving; 1.5 x 10 = 15. Multiplying by 4 again is the trap.

redirect_script.stop: You found k — now what do you DO with it?
redirect_script.prompt: The equation is y = k times x. To predict, MULTIPLY your constant by the new amount — not add, not reuse the old numbers. Write y = (your k)(new x) and compute.
redirect_script.praise: You drove the equation to a new input — multiplying by k is exactly how proportional prediction works.

vocabulary.definition: Use the equation y = kx to find an output for an input that wasn't listed.
The proportional equation; multiply the constant k by any input x to get the output.

next_steps.if_pass: Ready for 7.RP.3 (write y = mx equations) and 7.RP.2 (percent applications).

worked_example_script.text: Write 'Fabric costs $6.00 for 8 yards, at a constant rate.'
First find k: cost per 1 yard. What do you divide?
6.00 / 8 = $0.75 per yard. So the equation is c = 0.75y.
Now predict the cost of 20 yards. Do we add, or multiply by the constant?
If a student writes 0.75 + 20 or reuses the 8 yards, point at the equation c = 0.75y and ask 'what does y equal now?'
Multiply: 0.75 x 20 = $15.00. The constant let us answer a question the problem never asked directly.
Your turn: 90 miles in 2 hours, constant speed. Find k, then predict the distance in 5 hours.

practice_problems.stem: If k = 5 and the equation is y = kx, what is y when x = 4?
A rate is $3 per pound. Write the equation for cost c and pounds p.
practice_problems.answer: c = 3p

practice_problems.stem: Apples cost $4.50 for 6 pounds (constant rate). Write c = kp, then find the cost of 15 pounds.
practice_problems.notes: Two-step: find k, then predict.

practice_problems.stem: A printer runs at a constant rate: 84 pages in 6 minutes. How many pages in 15 minutes?
practice_problems.answer: k = 14 pages/min; 14 x 15 = 210 pages
practice_problems.notes: Predict a value not in the problem.

practice_problems.stem: Sam used a constant of proportionality to make a prediction. Find and fix his mistake.
shown_work: Trail mix costs $0.40 per ounce. Sam wants the cost of 26 ounces.
practice_problems.answer: Prediction with a constant means MULTIPLY, not add: c = 0.40 x 26 = $10.40. Sam added the constant to the weight, which breaks the equation c = 0.40w.
practice_problems.notes: Canonical error: adding instead of multiplying by k.

practice_problems.stem: At a constant rate, 3 workers build 2 sheds. Using the same rate, how many sheds do 12 workers build? (k = sheds per worker)
practice_problems.answer: k = 2/3 shed per worker; (2/3) x 12 = 8 sheds
practice_problems.notes: k is a fraction; still multiply by the new input.

practice_problems.stem: A car uses gas proportionally and goes 96 miles on 3 gallons. A trip is 400 miles. About how many gallons are needed? Explain which quantity you multiply.
practice_problems.answer: k = 32 miles per gallon, so gallons = miles / k = 400 / 32 = 12.5 gallons. Here you divide by k because you're going from miles back to gallons.
practice_problems.notes: Reversed use of the constant — predict the INPUT from an output.

practice_problems.stem: Two proportional plans: Plan A charges $0.50 per mile, Plan B charges $0.45 per mile. For a 60-mile trip, how much do you save with Plan B? Show the equations.
practice_problems.notes: Two predictions plus a comparison.

activities.title: Find k, Then Drive It
activities.instructions:
1. Draw a context card ('$5.60 for 8 pounds').
2. Fill the sheet in order: compute k (per 1), write the equation y = kx, then answer a prediction question on the card ('cost of 22 pounds?').
3. The prediction line must show a MULTIPLICATION by k — no adding.
4. Swap sheets with another pair and check each other's equation and prediction.
5. Debrief: why does prediction always multiply the constant by the new amount?

activities.title: Add or Multiply?
activities.instructions:
1. Read Sam's prediction: c = 0.40 + 26 = $26.40 for 26 ounces at $0.40/ounce.
2. Decide whether $26.40 is a reasonable cost for 26 ounces and say why it isn't.
3. Redo the prediction using the equation c = 0.40w.
4. Write the rule: to predict with a constant, you ____ (not ____).

content.worked_problem: Trail mix is $0.40 per ounce. Cost of 26 ounces? Sam wrote c = 0.40 + 26 = $26.40.
content.error_step: Sam added the constant and the weight instead of multiplying.
content.why: The equation is c = 0.40w, so c = 0.40 x 26 = $10.40. Adding ignores the per-ounce structure.

activities.title: Prediction Relay
activities.instructions:
1. Team draws a card and must, in order: state k, write y = kx, and give a prediction for a new input.
2. Each correct step earns a point; a wrong prediction that came from a right k earns partial credit.
3. Pass the card to the next student for the next round's new input.
4. Fastest team with all-correct predictions wins.
5. Debrief the card that tripped teams up — where did the structure y = kx get lost?

strategy_links.why: The find-k-then-predict arc is a natural I Do / We Do / You Do sequence, each stage adding one step of the multi-step task.
The add-instead-of-multiply error is a clean, high-frequency mistake for a find-and-fix routine.
A journal prompt ('why does prediction multiply by k?') consolidates the meaning of the constant as an engine for the whole relationship.

questioning_prompts: What is k here, and what does it mean in the story (per what)?
Write the equation y = kx for this situation — what's your k?
To predict, do you add or multiply? By which number?
Your prediction — is it a sensible size compared to the given values?
How could you use k to go backward, from an output to an input?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student finds k, then adds it to the new input or reuses the original quantity instead of multiplying.
misconception_redirects.say: The equation is y = k times x. To predict, MULTIPLY your constant by the new amount — not add, not reuse the old numbers. Write y = (your k)(new x) and compute.
misconception_redirects.praise: You drove the equation to a new input — multiplying by k is exactly how proportional prediction works.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student uses the total from the original pair (e.g., multiplies by 7 oz again) rather than the new input.
misconception_redirects.say: The original 7 ounces already gave us k. For a new question, plug the NEW amount into y = kx.
misconception_redirects.praise: You used k with the new input — the old numbers were just there to find k.

quick_checks.prompt: k = 0.50 dollars per mile. Cost of a 30-mile trip?
quick_checks.look_for: $15 (0.50 x 30). An answer of 30.50 diagnoses adding instead of multiplying.

quick_checks.prompt: A car goes 60 miles in 2 hours at constant speed. How far in 5 hours?
quick_checks.look_for: 150 miles (k = 30, then 30 x 5). Reusing 2 hours or adding signals lost structure.

sentence_starters: To predict, I multiply k by the new input: ___ x ___ = ___.

worked_solution.stem: The cost of cashews is proportional to weight: 6 ounces cost $4.20. What does 22 ounces cost?

steps.annotation: Find the constant of proportionality first — dollars per 1 ounce.
The constant becomes the multiplier in y = kx.
Predict by multiplying k by the NEW weight, 22 ounces.
A value the problem never listed, found with the constant.

faded_example.stem: A drone flies at a constant speed: 45 meters in 5 seconds. How far in 12 seconds?

steps.annotation: Meters per 1 second — the constant.
The constant is the multiplier of time.
Compute k, then set up d = k x 12.
Multiply to predict the distance at 12 seconds.

diagnostic_flow.description: Start with S3, computing k as y divided by x, the At-proficiency core of the standard. If they pass, push forward to S5 (read k from equations and graphs) and S6 (interpret and predict). If they fail, drop below grade level: B1 checks whether they can divide a total by a number of units to make a per 1 amount, and B2 checks fraction division, the two grade 6 skills this standard's arithmetic leans on. If those wobble, the foundations F1 (division as equal sharing) and F2 (a fraction as a division) locate the gap in grades 3 to 5. S1, S2, and S4 remain available to probe the standard's own proportionality gate, (1, r) recognition, and fractional-quantity work.
